body:
The Pallavas in South Indian History

The Pallavas were an important ruling dynasty of South India. Although their earlier history extends back several centuries, their political and architectural achievements are especially well documented from the 6th to the 8th centuries CE. They remained an important power in the Tamil region into the 9th century.

The Pallavas ruled parts of present-day Tamil Nadu and adjoining areas of southern India. Their kingdom extended, at different times, from the region around Kanchipuram towards the Kaveri delta. Their position in this region brought them into frequent conflict with other South Indian powers, particularly the Chalukyas of the Deccan.

Kanchipuram: The Pallava Capital

Kanchipuram, also called Kanchi, was the principal capital of the Pallavas. It is located in present-day Tamil Nadu. Kanchi was both a political centre and an important centre of religion and learning.

The Pallava kings encouraged temple construction. Kanchipuram became especially significant for the development of South Indian temple architecture. The Kailasanatha Temple, associated with the later Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman II, is an important surviving example.

Mahabalipuram: The Pallava Port

Mahabalipuram, also known as Mamallapuram, is situated on the Coromandel Coast of Tamil Nadu, beside the Bay of Bengal. It was an important port town under the Pallavas.

The two places had different functions. Kanchipuram served as the principal royal capital, whereas Mahabalipuram was a coastal centre of trade and artistic activity. Its famous rock-cut monuments and temples were created under Pallava patronage.

The name Mamallapuram is associated with the title Mamalla of the Pallava ruler Narasimhavarman I. Mamalla means a great wrestler or warrior.

The Pallavas and Their Deccan Neighbours

The major northern rival of the Pallavas was the Early Western Chalukya dynasty, commonly called the Chalukyas of Badami. Their kingdom was centred in the Deccan, particularly in parts of present-day Karnataka. Their capital during the reign of Pulakeshin II was Vatapi, now called Badami.

Aihole was another important Chalukya centre, known for temples and inscriptions. The Chalukyas controlled important territories in the region between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.

The Pallavas and Chalukyas repeatedly fought over territory and attacked each other's prosperous centres. Their rivalry was an important feature of South Indian politics during the 7th century CE.

Prelims focus

  • Pallava capital: Kanchipuram or Kanchi, Tamil Nadu.
  • Pallava port: Mahabalipuram or Mamallapuram, on the Coromandel Coast.
  • Major rival dynasty: The Chalukyas of Badami.
  • Chalukya capital during Pulakeshin II's reign: Vatapi, now Badami in Karnataka.
  • Mamallapuram: Named after the title Mamalla of Narasimhavarman I.
  • Trap: Mahabalipuram was not the principal Pallava capital; Kanchipuram was.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 11, New Empires and Kingdoms, printed pp. 115–117, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 83–84; Archaeological Survey of India, Group of Monuments Mahabalipuram (1984), consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, Brief Synthesis, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: The Pallavas: Their Kingdom, Capital and Historical Setting

body:
Three Important Pallava Rulers

For understanding the Pallavas and Mahabalipuram, three rulers are particularly important: Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I and Narasimhavarman II. Their reigns explain both the conflict with the Chalukyas and the development of Pallava temples.

Pallava rulerApproximate reignPrincipal association
Mahendravarman I600–630 CEEarly Pallava rock-cut temples; conflict with Pulakeshin II
Narasimhavarman I630–668 CETitle Mamalla; victory over Pulakeshin II; monuments at Mamallapuram
Narasimhavarman II700–728 CETitle Rajasimha; Shore Temple and Kailasanatha Temple

These reign dates are approximate historical ranges. Their order and associations are more important than treating each boundary year as an exact, undisputed date.

Mahendravarman I and Pulakeshin II

Mahendravarman I was a Pallava ruler associated with the early development of rock-cut temple architecture. During his reign, the Pallavas faced a powerful opponent in Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty.

Pulakeshin II expanded Chalukya power in the Deccan. He attacked Pallava territory and achieved military success against Mahendravarman I. The Pallava ruler was forced to take shelter behind the defensive walls of Kanchipuram during the Chalukya advance.

The rivalry was not simply a personal conflict between 2 kings. Both dynasties wanted to preserve and expand their territories. Prosperous towns, important routes and politically valuable regions made their neighbouring lands attractive targets.

Narasimhavarman I: Mamalla

Narasimhavarman I succeeded his father Mahendravarman I around 630 CE. He was also known by the title Mamalla.

Narasimhavarman I reversed the earlier military setback suffered by the Pallavas. His forces defeated Pulakeshin II and advanced into Chalukya territory.

A major achievement was the capture of Vatapi (Badami), the Chalukya capital, around 642 CE. Following this victory, Narasimhavarman I acquired the title Vatapikonda, meaning conqueror of Vatapi.

The important ruler-title distinction

Narasimhavarman I = Mamalla = Vatapikonda. Mamalla is associated with the name Mamallapuram, while Vatapikonda commemorates his victory over Vatapi.

The Sequence of the Pallava-Chalukya Conflict

The central military events can be understood in chronological order.

  1. Chalukya advance: Pulakeshin II attacked Pallava territory during the reign of Mahendravarman I and achieved military success.
  2. Pallava response: Narasimhavarman I, the successor of Mahendravarman I, defeated Pulakeshin II.
  3. Capture of Vatapi: Around 642 CE, Pallava forces captured the Chalukya capital, marking a major reversal in the conflict.

The capture of Vatapi did not permanently eliminate the Chalukya dynasty. Chalukya power subsequently recovered, and conflict between the 2 dynasties continued.

Narasimhavarman II: Rajasimha

Narasimhavarman II, also known as Rajasimha, ruled later, around 700–728 CE. He is especially remembered for the construction of major structural stone temples.

His important architectural associations include the Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram and the Kailasanatha Temple at Kanchipuram.

Narasimhavarman I and Narasimhavarman II must not be confused. The first was associated with the defeat of Pulakeshin II and the great rock-cut monuments at Mamallapuram. The second was associated with the later phase of large structural temple construction.

Prelims focus

  • Mahendravarman I: Pallava ruler who faced the Chalukya Pulakeshin II.
  • Narasimhavarman I: Known as Mamalla and Vatapikonda.
  • Capture of Vatapi: Around 642 CE, under Narasimhavarman I.
  • Narasimhavarman II: Known as Rajasimha.
  • Rajasimha: Associated with the Shore Temple and Kailasanatha Temple.
  • Trap: Mamalla and Rajasimha were not titles of the same ruler.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 11, New Empires and Kingdoms, printed pp. 115–116, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 83–84; K. R. Srinivasan, Cave-Temples of the Pallavas, Archaeological Survey of India, 1964, section Narasimhavarman I Mamalla; Archaeological Survey of India, Group of Monuments Mahabalipuram (1984), consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Important Pallava Rulers and Their Rivalry with the Chalukyas

body:
Why Mahabalipuram Is Important

Mahabalipuram, or Mamallapuram, is one of the most important surviving centres of Pallava art and architecture. Situated on the Coromandel Coast of Tamil Nadu, it was a port town associated with the Pallava rulers.

Its monuments were created mainly during the 7th and 8th centuries CE. They show how Pallava builders produced different types of temples and sculptures using natural rock and carefully prepared stone blocks.

Most of the major rock-cut monuments are associated with Narasimhavarman I, also called Mamalla. Important structural temples, especially the Shore Temple, belong to the later period associated with Narasimhavarman II, or Rajasimha.

The Main Types of Monuments

The monuments of Mahabalipuram can be understood through their method of construction and their physical appearance.

1. Monolithic Rathas

The rathas are free-standing, temple-shaped monuments carved from large natural boulders. Monolithic means made from a single piece of stone.

The famous Pancha Rathas, or Five Rathas, demonstrate different early temple forms. They are among the best-known monuments of Mahabalipuram.

2. Rock-Cut Cave Temples

The mandapas are cave sanctuaries created by excavating spaces into existing rock. Unlike a free-standing ratha, a cave temple forms part of the rock mass from which its interior has been cut.

Important examples include the Varaha Mandapa and the Mahishasuramardini Mandapa. These monuments are associated with the Pallava tradition of rock-cut architecture.

3. Open-Air Rock Reliefs

A rock relief is a sculptured scene in which figures project from a larger stone surface instead of standing completely separate from it.

Mahabalipuram contains a famous large open-air relief known as the Descent of the Ganges, also commonly called Arjuna's Penance. It is distinct from both the rathas and the cave temples because it is primarily a sculptured scene on an exposed rock face.

4. Structural Stone Temples

A structural temple is built by assembling prepared building materials, including individual stone blocks. This differs from cutting a temple directly from one existing rock mass.

The Shore Temple is the principal example at Mahabalipuram. It belongs to the later Pallava period associated with Narasimhavarman II.

Recognise the construction type

  • Ratha: A free-standing temple form cut from a single boulder.
  • Mandapa: A sanctuary excavated into existing rock.
  • Rock relief: A sculptured scene on a rock surface.
  • Shore Temple: A temple complex constructed using separate stone blocks.

UNESCO World Heritage Recognition

UNESCO inscribed the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram on the World Heritage List in 1984.

The UNESCO property includes the Pallava rock-cut cave temples, monolithic rathas, open-air reliefs, structural temples and associated remains. It was still listed as a World Heritage property at the content cutoff of 18 November 2026.

The World Heritage designation applies to the Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, not to a separate World Heritage property named only after the Shore Temple or the Five Rathas.

Prelims focus

  • Location: Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu, on the Coromandel Coast.
  • Dynasty: Pallava.
  • Major period: 7th–8th centuries CE.
  • Five Rathas: Monolithic temple-shaped monuments.
  • Descent of the Ganges: Famous open-air rock relief.
  • UNESCO inscription: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, 1984.

[Sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, Description and Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 18 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Group of Monuments Mahabalipuram (1984), consulted 18 November 2026; Ministry of Culture, Government of India, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 83–85.]

body:
What Are the Pancha Rathas?

The Pancha Rathas, also called the Five Rathas, are a group of important monolithic monuments at Mahabalipuram.

Each ratha has been carved from a large piece of natural rock. The builders removed unwanted stone to produce a temple-shaped structure. This makes the rathas examples of monolithic rock-cut architecture.

The word ratha means chariot. The monuments received this name because their forms resemble temple chariots. However, they are stone architectural monuments rather than actual wheeled vehicles.

The Five Rathas are generally associated with the reign of Narasimhavarman I, or Mamalla, during the 7th century CE. Their different forms demonstrate the development of early South Indian temple architecture.

Names of the Five Rathas

The monuments are conventionally named after characters from the Mahabharata. These are the 5 Pandava brothers and Draupadi.

There are 5 principal ratha monuments in the group because Nakula and Sahadeva share a combined ratha name.

RathaBasic architectural formIdentification
Dharmaraja RathaSquare plan with a 3-storeyed pyramidal towerOne of the most elaborate rathas
Bhima RathaRectangular plan with a long, wagon-vaulted roofRecognisable by its elongated roof
Arjuna RathaSquare plan with a 2-storeyed towerSmaller tiered temple form
Draupadi RathaSmall, square, hut-like structureSimple shrine form resembling a traditional hut
Nakula-Sahadeva RathaApsidal plan with a rounded rearAlso called an elephant-backed form

Apsidal describes a building whose plan has a rounded end. A vimana is the tower rising above the main shrine in South Indian temple architecture.

The differences among the rathas are significant because they show that Pallava builders were working with several temple shapes, rather than producing identical monuments.

Why They Have Mahabharata Names

The names Dharmaraja, Bhima, Arjuna, Draupadi and Nakula-Sahadeva are traditional names associated with the Mahabharata characters.

The rathas were not built by the Pandavas. Their names do not establish a historical connection between the monuments and the events described in the epic.

The monuments belong to the Pallava period, many centuries later than the period traditionally associated with the Mahabharata narrative.

A common distinction

The Five Rathas are Pallava monuments with Mahabharata-based names. The names identify the monuments; they do not identify their historical builders.

How the Rathas Differ from the Shore Temple

The Five Rathas and the Shore Temple are both located at Mahabalipuram, and both belong to the Pallava architectural tradition. However, they differ in construction and principal royal association.

  • Five Rathas: Monolithic monuments carved from individual large rocks; principally associated with Narasimhavarman I.
  • Shore Temple: A structural temple complex assembled from stone blocks; principally associated with Narasimhavarman II.

This difference is important because a question may correctly identify both groups as Pallava monuments while testing whether they are monolithic or structural.

Prelims focus

  • Pancha Rathas: Located at Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu.
  • Dynasty: Pallava.
  • Ruler associated with them: Narasimhavarman I, or Mamalla.
  • Construction: Each ratha was carved from a single large rock.
  • Dharmaraja Ratha: 3-storeyed pyramidal form.
  • Bhima Ratha: Long, wagon-vaulted roof.
  • Trap: The 5 rathas were not constructed by the Mahabharata characters after whom they are named.

[Sources: Archaeological Survey of India, Group of Monuments Mahabalipuram (1984), sections on the monolithic temples and Five Rathas, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram, Outstanding Universal Value, section The Rathas, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, printed p. 124, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 83–85.]
